The core innovation lies in modeling race dynamics through hierarchical cubic B-splines, enabling frame-level simulation of multi-competitor races. Each horse’s trajectory is represented as a smooth function of time, parameterized by spline coefficients that vary stochastically across horses. These coefficients follow a multivariate normal distribution, capturing both individual variation and shared population-level trends. Spatial covariates such as drafting exposure are incorporated via a CFD-derived function, which maps relative positions into aerodynamic benefits. The generative nature allows forward simulation of entire races by sampling from the posterior predictive distribution of these splines. This enables counterfactual analysis—such as altering lane assignments—by intervening on the model inputs. The win probability is then estimated as the proportion of simulations in which a given horse finishes first. The method assumes that race dynamics can be captured by smooth trajectories and that CFD-derived drafting is transferable to real-world conditions. The framework is robust to noise in tracking data due to its probabilistic structure and can be adapted to other domains like sports analytics by replacing horse-specific parameters with player/team-specific ones.
